 Print In 1998, Morgan Freeman finally completed his Mississippi dream home after a two-year construction ordeal(Image Credit: Instagram) Morgan Freeman had spent years building a career in Hollywood, but when it came to choosing a place to call home, he wanted to return to Mississippi. Not New York, not Los Angeles. Mississippi, where he had grown up and where the land carried memories of his family. Getting the house built, however, was another story. Freeman and his wife, Myrna Colley-Lee, had sold their Manhattan condo before starting the project. What should have been an exciting new chapter turned into a two-year wait, with the architect and contractor reportedly failing to finish the house. Journalist Jim Auchmutey revisited the story in The Atlanta Journal-Constitution on 1 July 2001, in a profile titled 'Sweet Home Mississippi'. It revealed just how much trouble Freeman had faced before he could finally settle into the home he had envisioned. Why Morgan Freeman wanted to return to Mississippi
 Morgan Freeman grew up in Mississippi during the 1940s and early 1950s, then left to pursue his career. Even after moving away, he continued visiting his parents. The state remained part of his life, regardless of where work took him. He married Colley-Lee in 1984, and the couple eventually sold their Upper West Side condo in Manhattan to build a home on land that had once belonged to Freeman's parents. For him, this was not simply a move to somewhere quieter. There was family history attached to the property, and he had a connection to the place that a new house in a celebrity neighbourhood could never quite offer. In a Washington Post profile published on 12 November 2005, Freeman spoke about his attachment to the region, explaining that Mississippi felt more like home than anywhere else he had lived. The property itself was a Mediterranean-style house on a ranch reported to span 126 acres. It was a considerable change from Manhattan, with open land, horses and room to spend time outdoors. The two-year construction ordeal
 Morgan Freeman's plans ran into trouble when the construction dragged on without the house being completed. According to the report, the architect and contractor had spent two years working on the project, leaving Freeman increasingly frustrated. He eventually summed up the experience with a comparison that made his irritation pretty clear. “You could have built a 40-story building in New York faster than we were building our house,” Freeman said. The project finally moved forward after he met Bill Luckett, a lawyer from Clarksdale, Mississippi, who helped him deal with the problems surrounding the construction. Luckett took over the project, and the house was completed in November 1998. A home that had taken far longer than expected was finally ready. But Freeman's connection with Luckett did not end once the building work was done. How the house led to a lasting friendship
 Luckett and Morgan Freeman eventually became business partners. In May 2001, they opened Ground Zero Blues Club in Clarksdale, a town closely associated with the blues. An Action News 5 report published on 9 June 2020 recalled how Luckett first met Freeman while helping him sort out legal paperwork connected to the Mississippi property. It is an interesting turn in the story. Freeman had needed help with a house that was going nowhere, and the person who stepped in became a friend and business partner. A frustrating construction job ended up opening the door to another part of his life in Mississippi. What life was like at Morgan Freeman's ranch
 When Atlanta Journal-Constitution visited the property in 2001, Morgan Freeman was enjoying the things the house had been built to make possible. The profile described him spending time by the swimming pool and riding his horses. Even the name at the entrance was personal. 'SONEDNA' combined the names of his stepfather, Son, and his mother, Edna. Mississippi was not an uncomplicated place for Freeman, though. In the same profile, he discussed the state's racial history and his disappointment after voters rejected a proposal to change the state flag. His attachment to the place did not mean ignoring its problems. Still, he had chosen to return, and the house gave him a base in the region that had shaped his early life. The building process had tested his patience, but by November 1998, the home was finally finished. And along the way, Freeman found a friendship that would become part of his life in the Mississippi Delta.
